issues.legal_issue: A transfer of excess vacant land made without the required filing and notification is null and void, and permission concerning different land does not validate the transfer.
material_facts: The claimant’s title depended on a sale of land declared surplus in ceiling proceedings.
The transfer occurred after the original order declaring the land surplus had been set aside and the matter remanded, but before any fresh order or notification concerning the excess land was made.
The required statement had not been filed and no operative notification concerning the excess land had been published when the transfer was made.
The authority had refused permission to transfer the disputed land because a suit concerning it was pending; permission later granted concerned land retained by the transferor, not the disputed land.
issues.conclusion: The transfer was null and void under Section 5(3) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976. The permission granted for different land did not authorize the transfer, so the claimant acquired no title on which to base the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(3) prohibits transfer of excess vacant land until the landowner has furnished the statement required by Section 6 and a notification concerning the excess land has been published under Section 10(1); a transfer contrary to that prohibition is null and void. Section 27 requires prior written permission for the specified transfers of urban or urbanisable land with a building, but permission for other land does not authorize the disputed transfer. The Court also applied Ritesh Tiwari v. State of U.P. in addressing the transferor’s inability to transfer land subject to ceiling proceedings.

rule.if: civil_title_suit and transfer_claimed_as_source_of_title and excess_vacant_land_transferred and statement_not_filed and notification_not_published

predicates.civil_title_suit: A claimant brought a civil suit seeking title-based relief concerning property.
predicates.transfer_claimed_as_source_of_title: The claimant relied on a transfer from an earlier holder as the source of the claimant’s title.
predicates.excess_vacant_land_transferred: The transferred land was treated as excess vacant land in ceiling proceedings.
predicates.statement_not_filed: The landholder had not furnished the required statement concerning the land before the transfer.
predicates.notification_not_published: No notification concerning the excess land had been published before the transfer.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a civil title suit relies on a transfer of excess vacant land made before the required statement and notification, the transfer is treated as null and void.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction over a suit that, despite its framing, in substance seeks resolution of matters arising under the land-ceiling regime.
material_facts: The claimant framed the suit as a challenge to an authority’s auction and sought declaratory and injunctive relief.
The claimant’s asserted title depended on the effect of ceiling proceedings, their abatement, and the validity of a transfer made during those proceedings.
The State and the competent ceiling authority, whose actions and proceedings were at the centre of the claim, were not joined as parties.
The governing regime provided for finality of decisions and appellate remedies, and the suit’s real substance concerned matters arising under that regime.
issues.conclusion: The civil court’s jurisdiction was impliedly excluded, and the suit was barred despite its framing as a challenge to the auction.
issues.legal_principle: Under the tests in Dhulabhai v. State of M.P., exclusion of civil jurisdiction may be implied where a statutory regime gives finality to tribunal decisions and provides adequate remedies. Competent Authority, Calcutta, Under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 v. David Mantosh applied those tests to hold that the Act impliedly excluded civil jurisdiction over matters arising under it. The Court also relied on T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal and later cases cautioning against artful pleading that disguises the real cause of action.

predicates.civil_suit: A party brought a civil suit seeking judicial relief.
predicates.real_dispute_arises_under_special_statut: The substance of the dispute concerns rights or proceedings governed by a special statutory regime, even if the pleadings frame it differently.
predicates.regime_provides_finality_and_adequate_re: The governing regime gives finality to decisions of its authorities and provides adequate remedies for challenging them.

issues.definition: When a civil suit in substance concerns matters governed by a regime that gives finality to its decisions and provides adequate remedies, the civil court lacks jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: In a special-leave appeal, the Supreme Court may consider a pure question of law going to jurisdiction even if it was not pursued in the intermediate appeal, and a party supporting a favourable decree need not file a cross-objection merely to challenge an adverse finding.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the suit in favour of the appellant but rejected the appellant’s objection to the civil court’s jurisdiction.
The appellant did not file a cross-objection on jurisdiction in the appeal before the High Court and the jurisdiction issue was not part of the High Court’s decision.
The appellant raised the jurisdiction objection before the Supreme Court in a special-leave appeal.
The issue was a pure question of law going to the root of the matter and could be decided without additional evidence.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was permitted to raise the jurisdiction ground before the Supreme Court, notwithstanding the absence of a cross-objection in the High Court appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 22 CPC, as amended, permits a respondent to challenge an adverse finding without a memorandum of cross-objection when supporting a decree in the respondent’s favour; a cross-objection is required when the respondent seeks relief against the decree. The Court applied the principles in Banarsi v. Ram Phal and S. Nazeer Ahmed v. State Bank of Mysore. Although Order XLI Rule 22 does not itself apply to appeals under Article 136, the Supreme Court may draw on its principles under its plenary jurisdiction and its power to do complete justice under Articles 136 and 142, as explained in Ramanbhai Ashabhai Patel v. Dabhi Ajitkumar Fulsinji and Jamshed Hormusji Wadia v. Port of Mumbai. A pure jurisdictional question may be raised at a later stage where it requires no further evidence, consistent with Bharat Kala Bhandar (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Committee, Vasant Kumar Radhakisan Vora v. Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay, Chandrika Misir v. Bhaiya Lal, and Most Rev. P.M.A. Metropolitan v. Moran Mar Marthoma.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and jurisdiction_ground and pure_question_of_law and no_additional_evidence_needed

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.jurisdiction_ground: A party seeks to argue that the lower court lacked jurisdiction.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The ground can be decided as a question of law without resolving disputed facts.
predicates.no_additional_evidence_needed: Deciding the ground does not require the parties to produce further evidence.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, the Supreme Court may consider a jurisdiction ground that is a pure question of law and requires no further evidence.
